title: Booker’s ‘The Reserve 2026’ Is Its Second-Ever Rye, Aged in Ex-Brandy Casks
summary:
Booker’s is releasing its second-ever rye whiskey as the label’s newest addition to its Reserves collection. Booker’s The Reserves 2026 is a limited-edition whiskey finished in apple brandy casks and flavored with cinnamon. The uncut rye, which was aged for over six years and bottled at 125.1 proof, is now available at retailers nationwide for a suggested retail price of $129.99. James B. Beam Distilling Co.-owned Booker’s newest release joins Big Time Batch, released in 2016, as the only two ryes in its lineup.

content:
Booker’s is releasing its second-ever rye whiskey as the label’s newest addition to its Reserves collection. Booker’s The Reserves 2026 is a limited-edition whiskey finished in apple brandy casks and flavored with cinnamon. The uncut rye, which was aged for over six years and bottled at 125.1 proof, is now available at retailers nationwide for a suggested retail price of $129.99.

James B. Beam Distilling Co.-owned Booker’s newest release joins Big Time Batch, released in 2016, as the only two ryes in its lineup. It is also the third whiskey of The Reserves collection, which the brand launched in 2024 with annual, limited releases to honor former master distiller Booker Noe’s legacy.

News of an apple brandy finish from Booker’s leaked earlier this year and spawned disapproval across social media, with devotees decrying the ultra-premium brand for leaning into gimmickry. But in a press release, master distiller Freddie Noe, grandson to Booker, says the inspiration behind the cinnamon- and apple-flavored rye came from his grandfather’s annual batch of apple wine.

Brand tasting notes for The Reserves 2026 highlight apple and seasoned oak on the nose. The rich palate opens with barrel char, vanilla, and caramel, leading to a finish of warm apple pie.

“This release is a very Reserves take on his recipe,” Noe says in the release. “A robust rye whiskey — the elusive Booker’s rye you all love so much — aged in apple brandy casks with some cinnamon sticks for added character.”

title: We Asked 11 Sommeliers: What Cabernet Sauvignon Offers the Best Bang for Your Buck? (2026)
summary:
You don’t have to pay top dollar to get an excellent Cabernet Sauvignon. This may not always be easy to mentally reconcile. Even though it’s common practice in most states to pick up a bottle of inexpensive Cab Sauv at the grocery store, the grape variety’s sophisticated reputation holds strong. So strong that the sight of a cost-effective bottle may unwittingly deliver the assumption that the wine is inferior to pricier labels. This is far from being the case. Wine shelves abound with exquisite Cabernet Sauvignons whose high quality may leave you wondering why their price point is so low.

The article We Asked 11 Sommeliers: What Cabernet Sauvignon Offers the Best Bang for Your Buck? (2026) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
You don’t have to pay top dollar to get an excellent Cabernet Sauvignon. This may not always be easy to mentally reconcile. Even though it’s common practice in most states to pick up a bottle of inexpensive Cab Sauv at the grocery store, the grape variety’s sophisticated reputation holds strong. So strong that the sight of a cost-effective bottle may unwittingly deliver the assumption that the wine is inferior to pricier labels.

This is far from being the case. Wine shelves abound with exquisite Cabernet Sauvignons whose high quality may leave you wondering why their price point is so low. These are the gems that deliver the kind of joy the expensive stuff can’t, because part of the mirth comes from knowing you don’t have to reach deep into your savings account to buy another bottle and share it with your friends.

The abundance of Cabernet Sauvignons populating store shelves can sometimes make it tricky to find these special bottles. Having a little guidance along the way can always help to alleviate the struggle, which is why we asked 11 sommeliers to share the Cabernet Sauvignons that provide the biggest “bang for your buck” to wine lovers. Here’s what they had to say.

The best ‘bang for your buck’ Cabernet Sauvignons, according to sommeliers:

  • 2019 Château Latour-Martillac
  • 2018 Heitz Cellar Cabernet Sauvignon
  • 2021 Château Cantemerle
  • Narrow Gate Vineyards Estate Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Gibbs Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Hess Persson Estates Iron Coral Estate Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Clos des Fous Grillos Cantores
  • Greenwing Columbia Valley Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Faust Cabernet Sauvignon
  • 2022 Fattoria il Casalone Pepi Lignana
  • Château Potensac
  • Château Soussans
  • Château Rauzan-Ségla

“I recommend the 2019 Château Latour-Martillac from Pessac-Leognan in Bordeaux. This estate offers excellent value for those wanting to explore Cabernet-dominant Bordeaux wines from the Left Bank. They were originally classified in Graves, a region just south of Haut-Médoc, in 1959 and their reputation as a top winery in the area continues. This wine pairs wonderfully with grilled meats, game, and roasted root vegetables with herbs.” —Jake Bennie, sommelier, Sepia, Chicago

“The 2018 Heitz Cellar Cabernet Sauvignon is an exceptional value, particularly for guests who want to experience classic Napa Valley Cabernet without moving into the higher price tiers. Heitz has an incredible history in Napa, and this wine delivers the structure and character you expect from the region while remaining beautifully balanced and approachable. There’s generous dark fruit, savory complexity, and enough acidity and tannin to make it especially compelling at the dinner table. It’s a bottle I can confidently recommend alongside a beautifully prepared steak at our restaurant because it overdelivers for its price point and represents Napa Cabernet exceptionally well.” —Scott Jones, sommelier, The Edge Steakhouse, Rancho Mirage, Calif.

“After years of high highs and low lows, the best place in the world to find value in Cabernet Sauvignon just may be Bordeaux. From Petit Château to Grand Vin, there’s a lot of relative value in the homeland, including the marvel that is Château Cantemerle, a Fifth Growth in the Haut-Médoc. Since 2021, the estate has undergone a massive upgrade in infrastructure, including satellite imaging that allows vine-by-vine farming decisions. The wines, which were already way too good for their $40 retail price, are catapulting towards a very bright future.” —Clayton Fox, wine director, Restaurant R’evolution, New Orleans

“One of my favorite things about wine is finding bottles that surprise people, and Narrow Gate’s Estate Cabernet Sauvignon does just that. Grown high in the Sierra Foothills from their certified biodynamic vineyard, it’s a beautiful expression of Cabernet that isn’t overly extracted or overly oaked. Dark cherry, cassis, and black plum are layered with spice and a subtle savory tobacco note, while great freshness keeps everything balanced. At around $45, there’s a lot happening in this bottle for the price. It’s a Cabernet that shows just how much quality, character, and value there is to discover in the Sierra Foothills.” —Allison Yonto, owner and wine educator, Tahoe Wine Collective, Tahoe City, Calif.

“Gibbs Cabernet Sauvignon is one of those rare Napa wines that seriously punches above its weight. There’s plenty of dark fruit — blackberry, cassis, and plum — but it’s balanced by cedar, spice, and a nice freshness that keeps it from feeling too heavy. The tannins are polished, there’s real structure, and it feels serious without trying too hard. What sets Gibbs apart is the value: This drinks with the depth, structure, and pedigree of Cabernet at twice the price. It’s classic Napa Cabernet, really well made, and a wine that consistently overdelivers for the money.” —Josh Onstott, sommelier, Josephine, Los Angeles

“For the best bang for your buck, I would go with Hess Persson Estates Iron Coral Estate Cabernet Sauvignon from Napa Valley. This wine has been becoming increasingly popular over the past year, and many stores in America and Europe have it in stock. It is deep ruby in color, complex yet accessible, designed for immediate enjoyment with the capability to age gracefully and be enjoyed for years to come. It opens with inviting aromas of anise, plum, tobacco, and a hint of chicory. On the palate, a firm backbone of tannin supports flavors that echo the nose, with bright red fruits layered with warm, savory notes. The finish balances richness with fresh fruit, creating both warmth and vibrancy in each sip.” —Georgi Stoianov, general manager, ARLO, San Diego

“I think the best bang-for-your-buck Cab is the Clos des Fous Grillos Cantores from Cachapoal, Chile, a high-elevation single-vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon. It offers a nose of purple fruit, black pepper, and dried herbs. It’s medium bodied with nice red fruit lift and great tannic structure on the finish. This can be snagged for probably $25, it’s exactly the kind of Cab I like to drink. [Soil specialist] Pedro Parra was involved in the early days of the winery, and while I’m very late to the Pedro Parra party, I love everything he’s done.” —Scott Stroemer, sommelier, Galit and Cafe Yaya, Chicago

“Great value wines produced in amounts large enough that consumers can easily find locally often come from underappreciated regions. A great example of this is Greenwing’s Columbia Valley Cabernet Sauvignon. Grown in the rain shadow of the Cascade Mountains and surrounded by a river system, this region benefits from a sunny and dry climate and a long growing season. Acidity and smooth tannins slowly develop and accompany vibrant black fruit, cocoa, baking spices, and a bit of fig. Small amounts of Merlot and Malbec, as well as a splash of Cab Franc, add Old World elegance. Ample aging in stainless steel and, primarily, neutral oak brings structure and refinement. Being part of the Duckhorn Collection, this wine is both a great value and widely distributed. I found it locally on our little island and am thrilled to include it on our wine list.” —Harlan Spiva, sommelier, Grand Hyatt Baha Mar, Nassau, The Bahamas

“Faust Cabernet Sauvignon from Napa Valley is one of the strongest values in the Cabernet category today. It’s a wine of layered fruit, refined tannins, and a balanced structure that drinks well above its price point. It delivers that classic Napa depth and polish while remaining accessible, making it a go‑to recommendation when our guests want exceptional Cabernet character without moving into luxury pricing.” —Lee Nevarez, sommelier, The National, Autograph Collection, Oklahoma City

“Currently, I am really enjoying the Pepi Lignana Cabernet; a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and Petit Verdot made by Fattoria il Casalone, a family owned estate. The 2022 vintage is aged for 12 months in second used barriques and six months in the bottle before release. A dusty nose underlined with black cherries, blackberries, and a touch of mint and tobacco. On the palate, the smoky herbaceous notes hit you right away followed by stewed black fruits with noticeably soft tannins balanced with great acidity. You can find this wine within the $25 to $35 range.” —Kisong Mun, wine director and assistant general manager, The Dearborn, Chicago

“I’m really digging Bordeaux as a current hot spot for quality Cab Sauv at amazing prices. They’ve had a string of great vintages, and there’s plenty of value both inside and outside the classified Growths. Château Potensac, Château Soussans, and Segla by Château Rauzan-Ségla are some of the current favorites we’re showcasing in our restaurants, but the possibilities from the region seem endless.” —Drea Boulanger, executive wine director, Spiegelworld, Las Vegas

content:
On Monday, Buffalo Trace Distillery announced the release of Elmer T. Lee 40th Anniversary Edition, the first uncut and unfiltered expression of the esteemed single barrel bourbon.

The bottle’s rollout comes alongside the launch of the distillery’s new bottle drawing system, which was developed to make limited-edition releases accessible to more visitors. Interested customers can register for the inaugural Buffalo Trace Bottle Draw from Sept. 15 through Sept. 17, and the Elmer T. Lee 40th Anniversary Edition will be available at the Frankfort, Ky., distillery exclusively for customers chosen in the lottery. On Sept. 22, a third-party partner will select names at random, who will then be able to purchase the bourbon onsite from Sept. 28 through Oct. 11.

As the name suggests, the new bourbon marks the 40th anniversary of Elmer T. Lee, a label designed to honor the former Buffalo Trace master distiller who changed the American whiskey landscape by releasing the first-ever single barrel bourbon in 1984. Buffalo Trace inaugurated the line with Elmer T. Lee Single Barrel Bourbon in 1986 and has been rolling out limited-edition whiskies under the label in the four decades since.

“For the first time, we’re sharing Elmer T. Lee Bourbon exactly as it comes from the barrel,” Erica Bovard, senior brand director of American Whiskey at Sazerac stated in a release. “By offering it uncut and unfiltered, we’re able to highlight the depth and character of the whiskey while staying true to the standards Elmer set.”

Brand tasting notes highlight dried fruit, nuts, and baking spice on a rich, full-bodied palate. The finish lingers with notes of crème brûlée and toasted oak.

The lineup’s first-ever uncut and unfiltered bourbon was bottled at proofs ranging from 124.8 to 138.6. It comes at a suggested retail price of $99.99.

title: Parker’s Heritage Is One of the Most Compelling Lines in Whiskey. What’s Next for the Label?
summary:
With roughly 2 million barrels aging in Kentucky, Heaven Hill is one of the Bluegrass State’s biggest whiskey producers. And after 90-plus years of operations, the company has started — or acquired — more than a handful of famous American brands. Elijah Craig, Evan Williams, Henry McKenna, Old Fitzgerald, Bernheim, Widow Jane, Mellow Corn, Larceny, Rittenhouse, Pikesville… the list goes on and on. Yet when it comes to pushing the envelope of whiskey, one label stands above the rest: Parker’s Heritage.

The article Parker’s Heritage Is One of the Most Compelling Lines in Whiskey. What’s Next for the Label? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
With roughly 2 million barrels aging in Kentucky, Heaven Hill is one of the Bluegrass State’s biggest whiskey producers. And after 90-plus years of operations, the company has started — or acquired — more than a handful of famous American brands. Elijah Craig, Evan Williams, Henry McKenna, Old Fitzgerald, Bernheim, Widow Jane, Mellow Corn, Larceny, Rittenhouse, Pikesville… the list goes on and on.

Yet when it comes to pushing the envelope of whiskey, one label stands above the rest: Parker’s Heritage. Now in its 20th year, the acclaimed series has become Heaven Hill’s go-to bottling for (mostly successful) trials across mash bills, production techniques, and maturation. To consumers, it’s marketed as both premium and experimental, a rare look at what one of Kentucky’s largest distillers has in the pipeline.

“It represents what can be possible in American whiskey with dedication and time,” says Rob Bramble, a longtime Parker’s Heritage fan who has collected nearly every release in the series. “Something that is all too fleeting these days.”

Of course, talking about Parker’s Heritage is virtually impossible without speaking about its namesake, the late Parker Beam. A sixth-generation distiller whose career with Heaven Hill spanned over 50 years, Beam’s impact goes well beyond a single series. But for many drinkers, Parker’s Heritage remains the most direct link to a legendary distiller.

Today, via both its inventive products and charitable link, Parker’s Heritage remains among Heaven Hill’s most coveted bottles — proven once again with the recent announcement of its highly anticipated 20th release. Predicting what’s next reveals much about how modern whiskey companies operate — and the complexities in how a large distillery innovates.

Parker Beam’s Storied Career

In 1946, Earl Beam left the Jim Beam distillery near Bardstown, Ky. and moved across town to Heaven Hill, at the time an 11-year-old whiskey upstart. He might not have known it at the time, but Earl’s move away from the family’s namesake company would impact American whiskey for generations to come. In 1960, Earl was joined by Parker, his 19-year-old son, and a sixth generation member of the Beam distilling lineage.

Earl retired in 1975, paving the way for Parker’s ascension to master distiller, just the fourth in Heaven Hill’s history. In that role, he guided production through some of the most tumultuous times in American whiskey history, including an industry-shifting glut in the 1980s. Along the way, he helped introduce now-iconic SKUs including Elijah Craig Small Batch in 1986 and several single barrel bourbons, at the time something of an oddity. In the early 1980s, Parker was joined by his son Craig Beam, who later assumed the role of co-master distiller.

Parker would also lead Heaven Hill’s production team through its darkest hour. On November 7, 1996, a fire destroyed seven warehouses, along with the company’s Bardstown distillery. Heaven Hill spent the next three years contract distilling with industry partners, eventually moving operations to the Bernheim Distillery in Louisville, which it acquired 1999.

Parker was instrumental in the transition. Notably, he sought to make efficient use of wheat, a grain integrated into Bernheim’s existing operations, but one Heaven Hill had never worked with before. Almost by accident, those decisions led to the resurrection of modern wheat whiskey.

His efforts didn’t go unnoticed. In 2001, Parker Beam was elected to the Kentucky Bourbon Hall of Fame’s inaugural class, alongside living legends like Elmer T. Lee, Booker Noe, Jimmy Russell, and Bim Samuels, Jr. And in 2016, the Kentucky Distillers Association (KDA) named its lifetime achievement award in his honor.

The Launch of Parker’s Heritage

In 2007, Heaven Hill launched what would become the most visible nod to that legacy: Parker’s Heritage, a premium series of whiskeys to be released annually. The first bottling featured 11-year-old small batch bourbon, bottled at barrel proof across three different strengths: 122.6, 127.4, and 129.6 proof. At the time, barrel proof products were still something of an outlier in American whiskey.

The second release was arguably even more striking due to its age: a 27-year-old blend of approximately 100 barrels, bottled at 96 proof. The line’s third release marked Parker’s 50th anniversary at Heaven Hill and included whiskeys across all five decades of his employment, from the 1960s to the 2000s.

In the two decades since, the series has become synonymous with innovation, be it via recipes, age statements, or cask finishing. A 2011 version finished bourbon in Cognac barrels, at the time still a fairly novel technique. The 2015 release showcased Heaven Hill’s early experiments with Kentucky malt whiskey. And at 24 years old, 2016’s 10th edition release was the oldest bottled-in-bond whiskey in history.

For some Bourbon Boom-era whiskey chasers, the series became highly collectible. Bottles are unique to each year, unlikely to ever be duplicated exactly.

“I decided to collect them all once I had managed to procure multiple releases in a row,” Bramble says. “[They] were never cheap by the time I was getting into whiskey. Also, I have this grand plan to open them all up side by side some day, but let’s be honest, I’ll never be able to get through that tasting alive.”

“It represents what can be possible in American whiskey with dedication and time. Something that is all too fleeting these days.”

While Parker’s Heritage quickly became a chase bottle, they weren’t all runaway hits. That’s best exemplified by 2018’s Orange Curaçao Finish, to date the most polarizing release in the entire series.

“The worst, and it isn’t even close, is the Curaçao [Finish],” says Bramble. It’s currently — and somewhat purposefully — the only bottle missing from his collection.

“Sometimes [the line] can get a little too experimental rather than showcasing the extreme quality it was founded on,” Bramble says. “But I would argue it was the gateway for a lot of other distilleries to start trying some different things.”

But even Orange Curaçao Finish has plenty of defenders. Among them is Conor O’Driscoll, Heaven Hill’s current master distiller.“My recollection of it was like, ‘This is literally an Old Fashioned in a bottle.’ It was obviously whiskey-forward, obviously lovely orange notes, but not too sweet,” O’Driscoll says.

Whether widely beloved or sometimes divisive, after nearly 20 years, Parker’s Heritage has become a harbinger of what Heaven Hill might have in store. Individual bottlings can give clues to future line expansions. When it was released in 2023, Parker’s Heritage Cask Strength Rye was Heaven Hill’s only barrel proof rye whiskey. That changed just two years later with the release of Elijah Craig Barrel Proof Rye, a now regular — and award-winning — permanent expression.

A Celebrated Series Finds New Meaning

Early in its history, Parker’s Heritage served as a way for Heaven Hill to flex its deep whiskey stocks. In 2013, the series gained meaning far beyond whiskey itself. That year, Parker revealed he had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a diagnosis he’d been keeping private since 2010. His public announcement came with the establishment of the Parker Beam Promise of Hope Fund, which raises money for ALS Association research and patient care.

That year’s Parker’s Heritage release — titled “Promise of Hope” — marked a transitional phase for the series. Starting then, Heaven Hill committed to donating a portion of Parker’s Heritage proceeds to the ALS Association. To date, the initiative has raised and donated more than $1.4 million.

Around 2014, Parker stepped aside from daily operations, becoming master distiller emeritus. He was briefly succeeded by his son Craig, who himself stepped away in late 2014 to focus on his father’s care. (After some time away from the industry, Craig Beam is now master distiller at Jackson Purchase Distillery in Western Kentucky.)

On January 9, 2017, Parker Beam passed away from ALS. His legacy lives on, via his indelible industry contributions, ALS-focused philanthropy, and the whiskey series that bears his name.

Parker’s Heritage 20th Edition

For the 20th edition of Parker’s Heritage, the Heaven Hill team wanted to release something special, a whiskey that would honor both the line’s innovative ethos and Parker himself.

According to O’Driscoll, the whiskey comes from a mostly standard production run of Heaven Hill’s core bourbon mash bill. But there was one significant difference: using the distillery’s standard sour mash process, the bourbon was made with backset from rye whiskey production. It’s a sort of fused technique Parker Beam himself lauded for added spice, though one O’Driscoll says is all too easy to miss.

“In 2025, we mashed 14 different mash bills. Some of those are mostly experimental, and some of those are already earmarked potentially to go into something.”

“[Y]ou have to be very deliberate about it because the production schedule says HH Reg, [our typical bourbon]. It doesn’t say HH Reg with the rye backset. It’s simply that the week before we made this bourbon, we were making rye, so the rye backset goes into the HH Reg.”

The bourbon — about 100 barrels of it — was distilled between October 2011 and January 2012, then aged across Rickhouses A, KK, L, and M. After 14 years, it was bottled at 118 proof. Bottles will hit the market this fall with an MSRP of $199.99. But as with many Parker’s Heritage bottles, retail markups are common.

How Parker’s Gets Made — And What Comes Next

While O’Driscoll is the contemporary face of Heaven Hill’s production team, he’s not the only one calling the shots. As with most new or special edition releases, Parker’s Heritage is shepherded by Heaven Hill’s innovation panel, which includes about a dozen employees.

“People think that I get to make the decision,” O’Driscoll says. “I do not. I get one vote. Everybody else gets one vote. And specifically for Parker’s, it has to be unanimous.”

The panel meets roughly every six weeks to taste, dissect, and discuss Heaven Hill’s broader innovation pipeline. According to O’Driscoll, they taste candidates for Parker’s Heritage two or three times per year.

“We might taste three or four different Parker’s [candidates] at a time, and these two are candidates for next year, these two are candidates for the year after, and so on. And that lineup can get shuffled as well because, ‘Oh, wait, this one is kind of reaching a really nice peak right now. We probably shouldn’t wait another year,’ or, ‘This one’s not ready yet. We should wait another year.’”

Samples are prepared, proofed, and often pre-blended by the production development lab in Bardstown, which is overseen by Tawnie Gootee, Heaven Hill’s longtime supervisor of quality assurance and master taster. Panel tastings are generally done in conversation with Gootee’s team. That creates a two-way street of feedback: samples go from warehouse to lab to panel, and ideas shuffle back from panel to the lab, warehouse teams, and brand leads. Those conversations can have major repercussions for Heaven Hill’s broader innovation strategies. A cutting-edge expression for Parker’s Heritage could eventually make its way to shelves in a more permanent fashion.

For O’Driscoll and the broader innovation team, the lineup’s main and ongoing challenge is novelty. The idea is that while some Parker’s Heritage releases may share DNA, none will ever be exactly the same. That team is constantly looking at new levers to pull when it comes to laying down experimental stock.

“We did just bring on a brand-new distillery that’s giving us some more strings to our bow,” O’Driscoll says, referring to Heaven Hill Springs in Bardstown, which came online in 2025.

“We talk about at Bernheim how we mash all six styles of American whiskey. Well, in 2025, we mashed 14 different mash bills. Some of those are mostly experimental, and some of those are already earmarked potentially to go into something.”

Five of Heaven Hill’s six core styles — bourbon, wheated bourbon, rye, wheat whiskey, and malt whiskey — have headlined at least one Parker’s Heritage. The sixth — corn whiskey — was first used as part of 2025’s American Whiskey blend, which also featured wheated bourbon and an experimental rye/malt mash bill.

O’Driscoll says anything and everything is potentially on the table, including bourbons made with heirloom or rare grain varieties. While he can’t divulge specifics from the current crop of Parker’s Heritage candidates, he’s open about the idea of an edition built around corn whiskey.

“We brought out the 20-year-old corn whiskey in the Heaven Hill Heritage Collection, but we’ve never done a Parker’s Heritage corn whiskey. I wonder if there’s something fun we can do there.”

“Again, we’ve got options.”

content:
Listening to orders while crowding around a busy bar can make it feel like the bar world has its own language. Though there are out-there terms like “make it skate,” even common words like “dry,” “neat,” and “on the rocks,” often carry a different meaning in a cocktail-slinging setting than in everyday life.

Some might recognize this lingo from movies, while seasoned drinkers might know each call by just hanging around the local watering hole. Even though these terms are widely accepted bar vernacular, their meanings aren’t always clear — though some definitions are pretty straightforward, others sound like the exact opposite of what they actually mean.

That’s why we compiled a list explaining 15 of the most common bar calls you might encounter on an average night out. Just as bartenders should master the terms to understand what drinkers want, everyday consumers should also familiarize themselves with these terms to better convey to those behind the stick exactly what they want out of their drink. From “dirty” to “wet,” here is the ultimate guide to popular bar calls.

The Most Common Bar Call Terms, Explained

Dirty

Most commonly associated with Martinis, asking for a drink “dirty” means adding olive juice to it. Drinkers might use additional adjectives to describe just how much olive juice they like, such as “a little dirty,” “extra dirty,” or “filthy.”

Dry

While it seems paradoxical to call any beverage “dry,” this term pertains to the sweetness of a drink, where “dry” translates to the opposite of sweet. The call is typically used when ordering a Martini, with “dry” indicating a preference for a boozier Martini that includes less vermouth. Consumers can specify the amount of vermouth with other modifiers like “extra dry” or “bone dry,” meaning very little to no vermouth.

Finger

A “finger” is a rough unit of measurement that equates the amount of liquor poured to the width of the bartender’s finger. Drinkers can ask for a “finger of whiskey,” meaning the bartender pours just enough whiskey in the glass so its volume matches the height of their finger resting horizontally at the bottom of the glass.

Mist

“Mist” means serving a spirit or liqueur poured over crushed or pebbled ice. For example, drinkers can ask for a “vodka mist” or “whiskey on a mist.”

Neat

One of the most commonly used terms when ordering a pour of a spirit, asking for a drink “neat” suggests you would like the spirit on its own without any other modifications — no ice, mixers, or other ingredients. The result is a room-temperature, uncut liquor.

On the Rocks

To ask for a spirit or a cocktail “on the rocks” simply means serving it on ice. Most commonly, the drink would be served in a rocks glass, poured directly over ice cubes. This call ensures a cold beverage that will slowly dilute.

Rinse

A “rinse” is part of a drink’s build. It means to pour a bit of a spirit into a glass, twirl it around so it coats the inner surface, and dump it out. Though this might seem wasteful, rinsing a glass with a potent spirit or liqueur like absinthe or peaty Scotch can add some serious complexity to the final drink. Plus, it makes for a theatrical moment behind the bar.

Shaken

Asking for a drink “shaken” refers to its preparation. Ordering a cocktail shaken entails that the ingredients are added to a cocktail shaker and agitated (by shaking) until well combined. This technique — typically employed in cocktails with citrus juice — leads to an aerated, frothy texture in cocktails like a Whiskey Sour.

Skinny

Ordering a “skinny” version of a drink means asking the bartender for a lower-calorie iteration. In such cases, the bartender may cut back on sweeteners or other sugary ingredients, such as in a Skinny Margarita.

Stiff

Just as your muscles stiffen up when sipping on a strong drink, ordering a drink “stiff” means asking for a more booze-forward cocktail. This might entail upping the proportion of spirit in the drink or using smaller measurements of one or more of the modifiers in the build.

Stirred

“Stirred” is the counterpart to “shaken.” Rather than building ingredients in a shaker tin to combine, the components of a stirred drink are poured into mixing glass — either with or without ice — and mixed together until combined. The result is a silkier, less bubbly texture than a “shaken” cocktail. Drinks that are stirred are usually more booze-forward cocktails like the Negroni and Old Fashioned.

Up

To order a cocktail “up” is a reference to both the preparation and glassware it is presented in. Instead of in a rocks glass, an “up” drink would be served in a stemmed glass. It is shaken or stirred with ice until well-chilled, then poured into a Martini glass, Nick & Nora, or coupe. The term “straight up” can also be used, though the term is a bit more loosely defined.

Virgin

A “virgin” cocktail is one without any booze at all. This call typically refers to drinks with ingredients that can be substituted with soda or other zero-proof ingredients, such as a Mojito, a Moscow Mule, or a Piña Colada.

Well

A “well” drink is one made using liquors placed in the bar’s “well,” the easy-to-grab, go-to spirits. The set of well drinks includes simple two-part quaffs like a Vodka Soda or a Rum and Coke. However, classic and more technical cocktails like an Old Fashioned can also be made with “well” spirits. In those cases, the build is the same but with more budget-friendly ingredients.

Wet

The opposite of “dry,” a “wet” Martini refers to one with a considerable amount of dry vermouth. Cocktail bars have their own Martini specs, but asking for one “wet” informs the bartender that you want more vermouth.

title: Southern Glazer’s to Pay $12.5 Million to Resolve Bribery Investigation with the DOJ
summary:
On Thursday, alcohol distributor Southern Glazer’s announced that it reached a resolution with the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Alcohol and Tobacco Trade Bureau (TTB) in a longstanding investigation related to improper payments and bribery. In the deal, Southern agreed to pay $12.5 million. With this resolution the DOJ has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with the distributor, and the TTB agreed to take no further action regarding this case. Last year, the U.S. government opened a federal investigation into the distributor regarding misconduct that occurred from 2016 to 2024.

The article Southern Glazer’s to Pay $12.5 Million to Resolve Bribery Investigation with the DOJ appeared first on VinePair.
content:
On Thursday, alcohol distributor Southern Glazer’s announced that it reached a resolution with the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Alcohol and Tobacco Trade Bureau (TTB) in a longstanding investigation related to improper payments and bribery. In the deal, Southern agreed to pay $12.5 million. With this resolution the DOJ has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with the distributor, and the TTB agreed to take no further action regarding this case.

Last year, the U.S. government opened a federal investigation into the distributor regarding misconduct that occurred from 2016 to 2024. Former employees allegedly handed out cash payments, gift cards, luxury goods, golf trips, flights, and resort bookings for retailers in California for better shelf placement of Southern Glazer’s products and other benefits in return. The DOJ also says the company took out false invoices to conceal the payments.

“We are gratified to resolve the investigation in this fashion, and to be able to focus on earning the trust of our customers, supplier partners, and employees through ethical business practices, strong compliance oversight, and accountability at every level of the organization,” Southern Glazer’s president and chief executive officer Wayne Chaplin said in a statement released on Thursday evening.

In addition to the $12.5 million payment, Southern Glazer’s agreed to reinforce the company’s internal guardrails to prevent future misconduct. In the release, the company stated it had already made inroads to improve its TTB compliance after the federal investigation surfaced and prior to reaching the agreement. Southern Glazer’s claims it bolstered its staff and implemented proactive auditing, among other measures. The statement also suggests the non-prosecution agreement includes “other obligations over the next two years,” though the company did not disclose what those entail.

“This case serves as an important reminder that industry members are accountable not only for their own conduct, but also for the actions taken on their behalf by third party affiliates,” Anthony P. Gledhill, assistant administrator of field operations for the TTB said in a statement from the DOJ. “Third parties, likewise, are responsible for any illegal activities they carry out on behalf of an industry member.”

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on harvest forecasts in France, Sapporo crossing the U.S.-Canada border, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • France braces for a record low harvest: After a growing season tempered by droughts and wildfires, producers in the country are expecting this year’s harvest to produce the lowest yields in 30 years. The French agriculture ministry forecasts a total of roughly 900 million gallons to be produced from this year’s harvest, a 6 percent dip year-over-year and a 17 percent drop from the average volume measured across 2021 to 2025.
  • Sapporo stokes the U.S.-Canada tariff fire: The Japanese brewer announced its plans to shift some of its brewing operations to the U.S. from Canada following the onset of a 50 percent tariff on Canadian beer. The move also comes after Trump issued a ban on Canadian alcohol imports, which is set to begin Sept. 29.
  • Dentist slashes world record Champagne sabrage: Swiss dentist Mirko Bozin broke the record for the number of Champagne bottles sabred in one minute. Bozin blew the tops off of 118 bottles in 60 seconds at a cutthroat tournament in Neuchâtel, Switzerland, breaking the previous record of 96 bottles that had been set just three months prior.
  • Kendall Jenner’s second bev-alc foray: The supermodel acquired a minority stake in U.K.-based functional beverage brand Trip.Trip launched in 2019 with cannabis-derived products but has since shifted its focus to other adaptogens, including non-psychedelic mushrooms.

Product releases to watch:

  • A new seat at the aperitivo table: The Campari Group, which dominates the Spritz sector with brands like Aperol under its wing, introduced a new aperitivo to the U.S.: Sarti. Though it was first founded in 1885, this marks its first appearance stateside, landing in markets nationwide. The blush-colored liquor blends blood orange, passion fruit, and mango flavors into a sweeter profile than the bitter qualities of Campari and Aperol.
  • Pappy to release 2026 Van Winkle Whiskey Collection: Crafted between the Old Rip Van Winkle Distillery and Buffalo Trace Distillery, this year’s lineup includes bourbons with age statements of 10, 12, 15, 20, and 23 years, along with a 13-year-old rye. Suggested retail prices range from $169.99 to $499.99. Bottles within the limited-edition collection will be available at select retailers and on-premise accounts nationwide.
  • Josh expands Reserve collection with Sauvignon Blanc: The California mega-producer added a Sauvignon Blanc from Sonoma County to its Reserve lineup. Josh Cellars Reserve Sonoma County Sauvignon Blanc is rolling out to retailers nationwide for a suggested retail price of $16.99.

content:
In 2026, it’s hard to think of a food that hasn’t been Dirty Martini-ified. The rise of the savory drinks trend over the past few years brought variations spiked with pickle brine, sungold tomatoes, and MSG, and flavors inspired by sour cream and onion chips, Greek salad, and brioche.

At Titán, the new bar and restaurant in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood, the tart, acidic flavors of escabeche are given the Martini treatment in the Dirty Root. But in making the drink, co-owner Ivy Mix and head bartender Sergio Sarmiento weren’t trying to follow the all-things food fad. Instead, they were looking to capture the signature briny flavors of a classic Dirty Martini while paying homage to the flavors of northern Mexico.

Titán is a collaboration between Mix and co-owner chef Alan Delgado. Both established themselves as masterminds of Brooklyn’s food and beverage scene in their own rights — Mix at bars like the beloved (and now-closed) Leyenda and Whoopsie Daisy and Delgado at Fort Greene’s Los Burritos Juárez, known for its hand-rolled flour tortillas and long lines.

Mix likes to think of a cocktail menu like a vinyl album: The whole should be better than the sum of its parts. Where the songs together to form a cohesive story in an old-school LP, the various drinks on a single cocktail menu should sing in harmony.

“When I make a menu, I have a spreadsheet of what kind of flavors we’re using, what kind of spirits we’re using, so I can see that I’m kind of covering the entire drink spectrum,” she says.

The Dirty Root was Titán’s answer to the Dirty Martini. While diners can order the classics, Mix likes to have her own versions of popular cocktails at the ready to point guests toward something new and unique.

“There are certain boxes that I want to check, so when people come in and ask for, for example, an Espresso Martini, we can say, ‘Do you want to try ours?’” she says. “The Dirty Root was the Dirty Martini box that we wanted to check.”

Though the Dirty Root resembles a Dirty Martini in its look and briny flavor, the ingredients are a far cry from the drink’s vodka-and-olive-brine roots. Bacanora — an agave-based liquor from northern Mexico’s Sonora region — and blanco tequila act as the base of the cocktail, with dry vermouth, carrot eau de vie, and carrot liqueur playing supporting roles. Rather than relying on the classic olives for the savory punch, Mix and Sarmiento looked to escabache, a piquant and spicy ensemble of pickled vegetables, usually including peppers, carrots, and onions, that’s a staple in many Mexican households.

“In pretty much all of the houses in Mexico, they have homemade chiles and vegetables in vinegar,” he says. “If you only have tortillas and beans, you can make tacos by adding the escabeche.”

Once the two brainstormed their vision for a Dirty Martini riff, Sarmiento began experimenting with making a carrot vinegar at home. While the root vegetables’ juice brings a burst of flavor on their own, Sarmiento needed to find a mixture that would complement the cocktail’s combination of liquors. After a series of trial-and-error, he landed on a blend of carrot juice, vinegar, sugar, and salt, with touches of turmeric and ginger.

“Then we put it all together, and you have this earthy, savory, northern Mexico-style Martini,” Mix says.

The striking drink presents in the glass with a bright orange hue and is served with a sidecar boasting a trio of garnishes: a lemon twist, a pickled carrot spear, and a cocktail onion. Mix shares that its appealing presentation spurs an onslaught of orders when it makes its way across the room, suggesting that it has somewhat of a “fajita effect” with customers.

“People definitely do that to this drink because the glass is sexy, it comes with a little sidecar, and the color is just really kind of light and beautiful,” she says.

The Dirty Root’s eye-catching appearance and complex flavor profile has propelled it to become one of Titán’s most popular orders. And consumers’ recent infatuation with Martinis — especially food-inspired ones — doesn’t hurt. But in conceptualizing the cocktail, Mix and Sarmiento never sought out to meet some kind of trend.

“There’s this fad going on right now, which is fine, where everything tastes like food,” Mix says. “Taking a food element was not the point. The inspiration for this drink is all of the flavors of the north of Mexico.”
